cues.text: Let's turn now to chapter three: version control and collaboration.
This is where we move from writing software to managing how a team writes it together, over time.
Begin with Git.
Git stores history.
Every change made to a project is recorded, so you can look back at what changed, when, and why.

Git also supports parallel development, meaning several people can work on different things at the same time, and it supports merging, which is the act of bringing those separate lines of work back together.
Alongside Git, teams usually use a remote host, such as GitHub or GitLab.
A remote host supports pull request reviews, often shortened to PR reviews, where teammates examine a change before it is accepted.
It also supports issues, for tracking work and problems; checks, which are automated validations; and permissions, which control who can do what.
Now, a distinction worth holding onto.
Centralised version control relies on a central repository, one main place where the history lives.
Distributed version control, which is what Git is, works differently: Git clones history locally.
That means each person's copy contains the history, not just a thin working snapshot taken from a central server.
What good practice looks like.
Commit meaningful, atomic changes.
Atomic means each commit is one coherent, self-contained change, not a jumble of unrelated edits.
Give each commit a descriptive message so that anyone reading the history understands the purpose.
Review changes and resolve conflicts, which arise when two lines of work touch the same material in incompatible ways.
Tag releases, so that a specific point in history is permanently labelled as a release.
Use a protected main branch, and apply an appropriate branch policy, so that the main line of work cannot be changed carelessly.
And avoid rewriting shared history without coordination, because if others have already based their work on that history, rewriting it underneath them causes serious confusion.
One more caution.
Version control is not a substitute for backups, for secure secrets handling, or for documentation.
Having a repository does not mean your data is safely backed up; it does not make it safe to store passwords or keys in the code; and it does not replace writing down how and why the system works.
Let's move on to collaboration.
Collaboration means coordinating people with complementary expertise toward a shared goal.
Follow it through the lifecycle, in order.
During requirements, stakeholders align their needs.
During design, architects, developers and security specialists are involved.
During implementation, the team uses code review and pairing, where two people work on the same task together.
During testing, the team shares acceptance results and defects.
At release, QA, operations and product coordinate.
And in maintenance, the team shares incident learning, so that lessons from problems feed back into future work.
Cross-functional ownership reduces handoffs and ambiguity.
When a single team holds the mix of skills it needs, there are fewer points where work is passed along and meaning gets lost.
To make responsibilities clear, we use RACI.
The letters stand for four roles.
R is Responsible: the person who does the work.
A is Accountable: the person who owns the outcome.
C is Consulted: those whose input is sought.
And I is Informed: those who are kept up to date.
You should assign defect triage, environment ownership and release approval explicitly, naming who holds each.
The reason is simple: a lack of owners causes governance gaps, where important decisions or tasks fall between people and nobody acts.
Finally, communication.
Communication may be synchronous, such as a meeting, a call, or an urgent incident, where people interact at the same time.
Or it may be asynchronous, such as a written issue, a pull request, shared documents, or recorded updates.
Asynchronous communication supports distributed teams and different time zones, allows focused work, and leaves durable decisions that can be found later.
However, urgent incidents may require synchronous escalation, because speed matters more at that moment.
Good communication has a clear structure.
State the goal, the context, the decision, the action owner, the due date, and the acceptance, meaning how everyone will know the work is done.

Beyond structure, several habits matter: active listening, respectful feedback, concise updates, shared terminology, conflict resolution, and psychological safety, which is the confidence that people can speak up without fear of blame.
Choose the channel according to urgency, complexity and sensitivity.
And do not expose confidential data in public channels.
Lastly, meeting minutes should record decisions and actions, not verbatim noise.
The point of minutes is to capture what was decided and who will do what, rather than every word spoken.
